newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian Abacha-for-president lobby gains strength.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian Abacha-for-president lobby gains strength.

text.p: A chorus of voices urging Nigerian military ruler General Sani Abacha to become an elected president is getting louder by the day and politicians believe this is a carefully scripted plan to prolong his rule.
"Even though he has not said he will contest it is obvious that he will not only contest but also 'win'," said Paul Adebiyi of the opposition National Democratic Coalition (NADECO).

"By not registering parties floated by those perceived as opponents, the military government long ago cleared the coast of all those capable of posing a problem to the plan for the head of state to become a civilian president," he added.
None of the five political parties registered in September to contest a series of elections set to usher in democracy next year is antagonistic to the military.

The first of such polls, the local council election, took place last month, putting into power in most town halls members of the United Nigeria Congress Party (UNCP) and the Democratic Party of Nigeria (DPN), the two parties which have publicly said they are willing to endorse Abacha as presidential candidate.

Shortly after the success of the two parties, Abacha's press secretary David Atta, who like his boss rarely speaks to reporters, told state radio that Nigerians should put pressure on the general to stand in next year's presidential vote.
Acting on Atta's cue, groups have sprung up in several parts of Nigeria, saying their sole aim is to try to convince Abacha to shed his army uniform and seek a popular mandate.

"Solidarity rallies" are now common even in the opposition heartland of the southwest to press home the idea that Nigerians want Abacha to follow the footsteps of other military rulers in West Africa who have turned themselves into elected presidents.

"The plot is clearly thickening," commented a senior Western diplomat who has followed the political crisis in Nigeria since 1993 when a presidential vote aimed at restoring democracy was annulled by former military ruler General Ibrahim Babangida.
Abacha, who had been the second most powerful person in the country since 1983 when the army overthrew civilians, seized power in November 1993 in the chaos that followed the annulment.
He promised a short tenure but unveiled a transition to democracy programme only after strong opposition to his rule from home and abroad because of alleged human rights abuses.
The latest call for the army ruler to run came last week from traditional rulers of eastern Nigeria.

After a well-advertised meeting, the traditional chiefs issued a communique, hailing Abacha for restoring public order and economic discipline and urging him to seek the presidency in order to continue the good work.
Prominent Nigerians such as Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the anulled 1993 poll, and former military ruler General Olusegun Obasanjo remain behind bars.
Some politicians have stayed clear of the transition programme.

But those participating seem to accept that the highest office will not become vacant in 1998 when Abacha has pledged to hand over power to an elected president and are opting to contest lesser offices.
Former oil minister Don Etiebet last week quit a party he founded and funded and which was to field him as a presidential candidate and joined UNCP, the party dubbed "Abacha's party".
Etiebet "has finally seen the light...that it is foolhardy to nurse presidential ambitions in this season", commented the independent Guardian newspaper.
According to Lamidu Adedibu, a leader of the DPN, "Abacha will not join any party to run for the presidential election."

"All the five parties will be his party since the parties may not necessarily field any candidate but adopt him as 'our candidate,'" Adedibu, who has been campaigning for an Abacha presidency told journalists in Ibadan in the southwest.
Nigerian newspapers prominently featured the report which one headlined "How Abacha will be civilian president".

"If all of us agree that the head of state should continue as a civilian president, therefore, General Abacha has won the election unopposed. He automatically becomes a democratically elected president," said Adedibu.
